concepts.title: The verb sein (to be) in the present
concepts.explanation: 'sein' means 'to be' and is irregular, just like English 'am/is/are'. Each person has its own form: ich bin (I am), du bist (you are), er/sie/es ist (he/she/it is). Learn each form separately.

concepts.title: du: informal 'you'
concepts.explanation: German has more than one word for 'you'. 'du' is the informal one, used for one person you know well: friends, family, children. Strangers and formal situations get a different, polite form, which you will learn later.

concepts.title: Yes/no questions: verb first
concepts.explanation: To ask a yes/no question, put the verb at the very beginning, before the subject. 'Er ist Robert.' (He is Robert.) becomes 'Ist er Robert?' (Is he Robert?). No helper word like English 'do' is ever needed.

concepts.title: sie: 'she' or 'they'
concepts.explanation: Lowercase 'sie' can mean 'she' or 'they'. The verb usually tells you which: 'sie ist' is 'she is', while 'they' takes a plural verb form. Capitalized 'Sie' in the middle of a sentence is the polite 'you', which comes later.

examples.text: Er ist Robert, sie ist Anna.

concepts.title: 'It's me': ich bin es
concepts.explanation: To say who someone is, German makes the person the subject and puts 'es' after the verb: 'Ich bin es.' (It's me.), 'Er ist es.' (It's him.). The verb matches the person, not 'es'. You can also say 'Es ist Anna.' (It's Anna.).

concepts.title: das: 'that/this' for pointing
concepts.explanation: 'das' is used to point at or introduce someone or something: 'Das ist Anna.' (This is Anna.). It works for people of any gender. In 'Das bin ich.' (That's me.) the verb matches 'ich', not 'das'.

concepts.title: Negation with nicht
concepts.explanation: 'nicht' means 'not'. It usually comes after the verb and before the word it negates: 'Ich bin nicht Anna.' (I'm not Anna.). With a pronoun like 'es', 'nicht' goes at the end: 'Er ist es nicht.' (It's not him.).

concepts.title: Verb in second place
concepts.explanation: In a German statement, the verb is always the second element. If something other than the subject comes first, the subject moves behind the verb: 'Ich bin hier.' but 'Hier bin ich.' (Here I am.). English sometimes does this too, but German always does.

concepts.title: ja as a flavoring particle
concepts.explanation: Besides meaning 'yes', ja is often slipped into a sentence (after the verb) to add surprise or 'as we both know'. It has no direct English equivalent; English uses 'why', 'oh' or 'after all'. Das ist ja Betty! means 'Why, that's Betty!'

concepts.title: nein vs. nicht
concepts.explanation: nein means 'no' and stands on its own as an answer. nicht means 'not' and goes inside a sentence to negate it. They often appear together: Nein, er ist nicht hier. ('No, he's not here.')

examples.text: Ist das Karl? – Nein, das ist Thomas.
examples.en: Is that Karl? – No, that's Thomas.

concepts.title: der / die as 'he' / 'she' in speech
concepts.explanation: In everyday spoken German, the words der and die are often used on their own instead of er and sie, a bit like 'that guy' or 'that one'. Der ist hier. means 'He's here.' It is casual, so use er and sie in careful speech.

concepts.title: Das sind ...: 'this is / these are' with plural
concepts.explanation: When das points to more than one person or thing, the verb becomes plural: das sind, not das ist. The verb agrees with what comes after it. Das sind Betty und Karl. means 'This is Betty and Karl.'

concepts.title: ihr: informal 'you' for several people
concepts.explanation: German has a separate word for 'you' when talking to more than one friend or family member: ihr (like 'you guys' or 'y'all'). du is for one person, ihr for several. Wir sind hier, und ihr? means 'We're here, and you guys?'

concepts.title: Sie: formal 'you'
concepts.explanation: German has a polite 'you' for strangers, customers and people you don't know well: Sie, always written with a capital S. It works for one person or several and takes the same verb form as 'they': Sind Sie Emily? (Are you Emily?). With friends and family you use du instead.

concepts.title: Questions with question words
concepts.explanation: Questions with a question word like was (what) or wie (how) put that word first and the verb right after it, in second place: Was ist das? (What is that?). This is the same 'verb second' rule as in statements; only yes/no questions start with the verb.

concepts.title: wie: 'like, as' in comparisons
concepts.explanation: wie compares two things: Er ist wie ich. (He's like me.) Notice that German keeps the same pronoun form after wie as before it: 'wie ich', where English says 'like me'. so wie means 'just like'.
concepts.notes: generated by claude-opus-5-5 (tools/generate.py, 2026-11-28) | REVIEW warning: Saying German 'keeps the same pronoun form after wie as before it' is confusing, since 'Er ist wie ich' has er before and ich after; the rule is about case. Suggested fix: 'The word after wie takes the same case as the word it is compared with, here nominative (ich, er), where English says me/him.' | REVIEW warning: The explanation mentions 'so wie', but 'so' is only introduced in the next entry (order 24). Move this remark to a note on 'Johanna ist so wie du.'

concepts.title: auch nicht: 'not ... either', 'neither'
concepts.explanation: To say 'me neither' or 'not ... either', German simply combines auch (also) with nicht: Ich auch nicht. (Me neither.) In a full sentence auch nicht usually stands together: Er ist auch nicht hier. (He isn't here either.)

concepts.title: The verb haben (to have) in the present
concepts.explanation: haben means 'to have' and is slightly irregular: ich habe, du hast, er/sie/es hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie/Sie haben. Example: Er hat es. (He has it.) German has no 'do' in questions or negation: Hat sie es? (Does she have it?), Er hat es nicht. (He doesn't have it.)

concepts.title: Possessives standing alone: 'mine'
concepts.explanation: When the noun is left out, the possessive word stands alone and means 'mine'. For a feminine noun or a plural it is meine: Das ist meine. ('That's mine.') For masculine nouns it becomes meiner, for neuter nouns meins.

concepts.title: Regular verbs in the present: ich -e
concepts.explanation: Most German verbs are regular: take the infinitive, drop -en, and add an ending. With ich the ending is -e: meinen ('to mean') becomes ich meine ('I mean'). Other persons get other endings, which you will meet step by step.

examples.en: I don't mean it like that.

concepts.title: und / aber don't count for word order
concepts.explanation: Linking words like und ('and') and aber ('but') sit in front of the sentence and don't take up the first position. After them, the normal order follows with the verb in second place: Aber er ist nicht hier. ('But he isn't here.')

concepts.title: noch nicht: 'not yet'
concepts.explanation: noch on its own means 'still', but noch nicht means 'not yet'. It goes where nicht would normally go: Er ist noch nicht hier. ('He isn't here yet.')

concepts.title: Adjectives after sein: no ending
concepts.explanation: When an adjective comes after sein ('to be'), it keeps its basic form, whatever the subject is. Das ist gut, er ist gut, wir sind gut: always just gut.

concepts.title: gut means 'good' and 'well'
concepts.explanation: German adjectives can be used as adverbs without any change; there is no extra ending like English '-ly'. So gut means both 'good' and 'well': Ich meine es gut. ('I mean well.')

concepts.title: der becomes den as an object
concepts.explanation: The thing or person a verb acts on is the direct object (accusative case). Only masculine words change: der becomes den, while die and das stay the same. Den habe ich. ('I've got that one / him.')

concepts.title: ein becomes einen as an object
concepts.explanation: Like der → den, the masculine ein becomes einen when it is the direct object. Feminine eine and neuter ein don't change. On its own, einen means 'one': Ich habe einen. ('I have one.')

examples.review: This example reuses 'Wir haben noch einen', which is translated as 'We still have one'; it more naturally means 'We have one more', so the example may mislead learners.

concepts.title: zu vs. auch: two kinds of 'too'
concepts.explanation: English 'too' has two meanings, and German uses two words. zu means 'too much, excessively': Du bist zu gut. ('You're too kind.') auch means 'also': Das ist auch gut. ('That's good too.')

concepts.title: kein: 'no', 'not a', 'not any'
concepts.explanation: German uses kein to negate nouns where English says 'no', 'not a' or 'not any'. Use nicht for verbs, adjectives and whole statements, but kein when you mean 'none of a thing'. Standing alone it means 'none': Ich habe keine. = I don't have any.
concepts.notes: generated by claude-opus-5-5 (tools/generate.py, 2026-11-28) | REVIEW warning: 'kein when you mean none of a thing' is vague. Clearer: kein negates nouns that would otherwise have ein/eine or no article, while nicht negates verbs, adjectives, names and nouns with der/die/das.

concepts.title: man: 'one', 'you', 'people'
concepts.explanation: man is a subject meaning people in general, like English 'you' or 'one'. It always takes the same verb form as er/sie/es: man ist, man hat. Hier hat man es gut. = You have it good here.

examples.en: You are the way you are.
Do people still have that today?

concepts.title: kann: modal verb + infinitive at the end
concepts.explanation: kann (can) is a modal verb. It takes the normal verb slot, and the main verb goes to the very end in its infinitive form: Kann ich einen haben? = Can I have one? The ich and er/sie/es forms are the same: ich kann, er kann. When the meaning is clear, the second verb is often left out: Ich kann das. = I can do that.

concepts.title: dass sends the verb to the end
concepts.explanation: After dass (that), the conjugated verb moves to the very end of its clause. Compare: Du bist hier. but: Gut, dass du hier bist. A comma always separates the dass-clause from the rest of the sentence.

examples.text: Es ist gut, dass er noch hier ist.
examples.en: It's good that he's still here.

examples.text: Gut, dass wir noch einen haben.
examples.en: Good thing we still have one.

concepts.title: mit takes the dative: mit mir
concepts.explanation: The preposition mit (with) is always followed by the dative case. For 'me', the dative form is mir, so 'with me' is mit mir, never mit ich. Er ist mit mir hier. = He's here with me.

examples.text: Lisa ist heute mit mir in Wien.
examples.en: Lisa is in Vienna with me today.

concepts.title: ich, mich, mir: three words for 'I / me'
concepts.explanation: German has three forms where English has 'I' and 'me'. ich is the subject, mich is the direct object (accusative), and mir is used after prepositions like mit and for 'to me' (dative). Ich meine mich. = I mean me.
concepts.notes: generated by claude-opus-5-5 (tools/generate.py, 2026-11-28) | REVIEW warning: Saying mir 'is used after prepositions like mit' suggests all prepositions take mir, but many take mich (für mich, ohne mich). Rephrase as 'after dative prepositions like mit'.

concepts.title: du, dich, dir: three words for 'you'
concepts.explanation: Like ich / mich / mir, informal 'you' has three forms. du is the subject, dich is the direct object (ich habe dich = I have you), and dir comes after prepositions like mit (mit dir = with you) and for 'to you'.

examples.text: Du hast mich, und ich habe dich.
examples.en: You have me, and I have you.

concepts.title: wo in the middle of a sentence: verb at the end
concepts.explanation: wo can also join two parts of a sentence ('where ...'). Just like after dass, the verb then goes to the very end of that part: Er ist in Rom, wo auch Daniel ist.

examples.text: Er ist in Rom, wo auch Daniel ist.
examples.en: He's in Rome, where Daniel is too.

examples.text: Sie ist in London, wo auch Stefan ist.
examples.en: She's in London, where Stefan is too.

concepts.title: da sein: to be here, to be around
concepts.explanation: da usually means 'there', but with sein it often means 'present, here, in'. Ist Stefan da? = Is Stefan here / in? Ich bin da! = I'm here!

concepts.title: von for possession: der von Stefan
concepts.explanation: In everyday German, von + a person often replaces English 's. Ist das der von Stefan? = Is that Stefan's (one)? Later you'll see it with nouns too, like 'the ... of Stefan'.

concepts.title: war: 'was'
concepts.explanation: war is the past of sein for ich and er/sie/es: ich war = I was, er war = he was. German often uses war in speech where English might say 'have been': Ich war noch nicht in Wien = I haven't been to Vienna yet.

concepts.title: Separable verbs: the particle goes to the end
concepts.explanation: Some verbs have a small front part that splits off and moves to the end of the sentence. anhaben (to wear) becomes: Was hast du an? = What are you wearing? The verb stays in second place, the particle goes last.

concepts.title: als: 'when' for one time in the past
concepts.explanation: als means 'when' for a single event or period in the past. Like dass, it sends the verb to the end of its part of the sentence: als ich in Berlin war = when I was in Berlin.

examples.text: Als ich in Berlin war, war Leanna auch da.
examples.en: When I was in Berlin, Leanna was there too.

examples.text: Ich war in Rom, als sie in London war.
examples.en: I was in Rome when she was in London.

examples.text: Das war, als ich in München war.
examples.en: That was when I was in Munich.

concepts.title: Clause first, then the verb
concepts.explanation: If a whole clause (with dass, als, ...) starts the sentence, it counts as the first element. So the main verb comes right after the comma, before its subject: Als ich in Berlin war, war Leanna auch da.

examples.text: Als ich in Berlin war, war Leanna auch da.
examples.en: When I was in Berlin, Leanna was there too.

examples.text: Als er hier war, war ich in Paris.
examples.en: When he was here, I was in Paris.

examples.text: Dass er das kann, ist gut.
examples.en: It's good that he can do that.

concepts.title: der / das become dem in the dative
concepts.explanation: After words like mit and von, German uses the dative case. Masculine der and neuter das both change to dem there. In speech, dem alone can also mean 'him' or 'that one': Was ist mit dem? (What's up with him?)

examples.text: Ich war mit dem in Berlin.
examples.en: I was in Berlin with him.

concepts.notes: generated by claude-opus-5-5 (tools/generate.py, 2026-11-28) | REVIEW warning: The title and explanation are about the article der/das becoming dem, but all three examples show only the demonstrative-pronoun use ('him'), so none shows the article change. Add a short explanatory line making clear that these examples are the pronoun use, until a noun allows a true article example like 'mit dem Mann'.

concepts.title: für takes the accusative
concepts.explanation: für means 'for' and is always followed by the accusative case. So you say für mich and für dich, not für mir or für dir: Das ist für dich. (This is for you.)

concepts.title: wenn: 'if' and 'when(ever)'
concepts.explanation: wenn means 'if', and also 'when' or 'whenever' for the present, the future, or things that happen repeatedly. Like dass, it sends the verb to the end of its clause: Wenn du da bist, bin ich auch da. For a single event in the past, use als instead.

examples.text: Wenn du da bist, bin ich auch da.
examples.en: If you're there, I'll be there too.

examples.text: Wenn ich kann, bin ich da.
examples.en: If I can, I'll be there.

concepts.title: aus: where you come from
concepts.explanation: To say where someone is from, German uses aus: Ich bin aus Berlin. (I'm from Berlin.) von is used for 'from' a person or a starting point, but for your home town or country it's aus.

concepts.title: wird: 'becomes, gets'
concepts.explanation: wird is a form of werden, 'to become'. It's used like English 'get' or 'is going to be' with an adjective: Das wird gut. (That's going to be good.) Er wird sehr gut. (He's getting really good.)

concepts.title: The future with werden
concepts.explanation: German forms the future with werden plus an infinitive at the very end: Er wird da sein. (He'll be there.) Often it also expresses a guess: Sie wird jetzt in Paris sein. (She's probably in Paris now.) In everyday speech the present tense is often used for the future too.

concepts.title: nach: 'to' a place, 'after'
concepts.explanation: nach means 'to' before names of cities and most countries: nach Paris (to Paris). It also means 'after': Nach dir! (After you!) nach is always followed by the dative case.

concepts.title: wir and uns: 'we' and 'us'
concepts.explanation: wir is 'we' as the subject. As an object, and after prepositions like mit, von and für, it becomes uns ('us'). Unlike mich/mir, uns is the same in the accusative and dative: für uns, mit uns.

examples.text: Er war mit uns in Rom.
examples.en: He was in Rome with us.

concepts.title: schon: reassuring 'surely, it'll be fine'
concepts.explanation: Besides 'already', schon is often used to reassure or to admit something is likely. Das wird schon means 'It'll be fine', and Das kann schon sein means 'That may well be'. It adds a calm, confident tone rather than a time meaning.

concepts.title: immer noch: 'still'
concepts.explanation: immer noch means 'still' (something continues). Er ist immer noch hier = 'He's still here.' Add nicht for 'still not': Sie ist immer noch nicht da = 'She still isn't here.'

examples.text: Sie ist immer noch nicht da.

concepts.title: mehr als: 'more than'
concepts.explanation: To say 'more than', use mehr als. Here als means 'than', not 'when'. Er hat mehr als ich = 'He has more than me.' Note that German uses ich (not mich) after als here.

concepts.title: nicht mehr / kein ... mehr: 'no longer'
concepts.explanation: nicht mehr means 'not anymore, no longer': Er ist nicht mehr hier = 'He isn't here anymore.' With kein, put mehr after it: Ich habe keine mehr = 'I don't have any left.' Ich kann nicht mehr is a common way to say 'I can't go on.'

concepts.title: vor: 'before', 'in front of'
concepts.explanation: vor means 'before' (in time or order) and 'in front of' (place). Like mit and nach, it takes the dative: vor mir, vor dir, vor uns. Er war vor mir da = 'He got there before me.'

examples.text: Wer ist das da vor uns?
examples.en: Who's that in front of us?

concepts.notes: generated by claude-opus-5-5 (tools/generate.py, 2026-11-28) | REVIEW warning: Saying vor simply 'takes the dative like mit and nach' is misleading: vor is a two-way preposition that takes the accusative with movement towards a place (vor das Haus). Suggest: 'For time and location it takes the dative.'

concepts.title: er and ihn: 'he' and 'him'
concepts.explanation: er is 'he' as the subject; as a direct object or after für it becomes ihn: Das ist für ihn = 'This is for him.' This is the same der → den change seen with articles. Because German nouns have gender, ihn also means 'it' for a masculine thing.

concepts.title: dieser / diese / dieses: 'this', 'these'
concepts.explanation: dies- means 'this' (or 'these' in the plural). It takes endings like der/die/das: dieser (masc.), diese (fem. and plural), dieses (neut.). It can come before a noun or stand alone as 'this one / these': Diese hier ist gut. = This one here is good.

concepts.title: bei: 'at someone's place', 'with'
concepts.explanation: bei means being at a person's place or with them: Ich bin bei Tom. = I'm at Tom's. It always takes the dative: bei mir, bei dir, bei uns. bei mir can also mean 'for me, in my case'. Note: bei is for being somewhere; going there uses other words.

concepts.title: wissen: ich weiß, er weiß
concepts.explanation: wissen (to know a fact) is irregular. ich and er/sie/es share the same form with no ending: ich weiß, er weiß (not 'er weißt'). It often introduces a clause: Ich weiß, dass du da bist. Ich weiß nicht, wo er ist. The verb in that second clause goes to the end.

concepts.title: muss nicht: 'don't have to'
concepts.explanation: muss means 'must, have to'. But muss nicht means 'don't have to', not 'must not': Es muss nicht heute sein. = It doesn't have to be today. It means something is not necessary, not that it is forbidden.

examples.en: It doesn't have to be today.

examples.text: Man muss nicht immer gut sein.
examples.en: You don't always have to be good.

concepts.title: will means 'want', not 'will'
concepts.explanation: German will looks like English 'will', but it means 'want(s)': Ich will das. = I want that. It's the ich/er/sie form of wollen and works like kann: other verbs go to the end. For the future, German uses werden (er wird), not will.

examples.en: She wants to go to Paris.

concepts.title: nichts: 'nothing'
concepts.explanation: nichts means 'nothing' or 'not anything': Ich habe nichts. = I have nothing. Don't mix it up with nicht ('not'), which negates a verb or word. German needs no extra 'not' with nichts: Er weiß nichts. = He doesn't know anything.

concepts.title: über: 'about' (+ accusative)
concepts.explanation: über often means 'about' a topic, and then it takes the accusative: über mich, über dich, über ihn. Ich weiß etwas über ihn. = I know something about him. über can also mean 'via' (über Wien) or 'over, above'.

examples.en: I don't know anything about her.
What does he know about me?

concepts.title: sein / seine: 'his'
concepts.explanation: The possessive for a male person (or a masculine/neuter thing) is sein, which becomes seine before feminine and plural nouns, or when it stands alone for them: Das ist seine = That's his. Don't confuse it with 'her', which in German is ihr, not sein.

concepts.title: er, ihn, ihm: three words for 'he / him'
concepts.explanation: Like ich / mich / mir, 'he' has three forms: er (subject), ihn (direct object) and ihm (dative). Use ihm after dative prepositions like mit, bei and von: mit ihm = with him.

examples.text: Ich war mit ihm in Wien.
examples.en: I was in Vienna with him.

concepts.title: einer: 'one' or 'someone' on its own
concepts.explanation: When ein stands alone without a noun, it takes the ending of der: einer for a masculine 'one'. Einer von uns means 'one of us', and Da ist einer can mean 'There's someone there'.

examples.text: Einer von uns muss hier sein.
examples.en: One of us has to be here.

concepts.title: ..., oder? : 'right?', 'isn't it?'
concepts.explanation: Put oder with a question mark at the end of a statement to ask for agreement, like English 'right?' or 'isn't it?'. It never changes: Das ist gut, oder? = That's good, isn't it?

concepts.title: hatte: 'had'
concepts.explanation: The past of haben is hatte, and it is the same for ich and er/sie/es: Ich hatte nichts = I had nothing. Like war for sein, hatte is very common in speech as well as writing.

examples.en: He had more than I did.

concepts.title: zu + infinitive: viel zu tun
concepts.explanation: After words like viel, nichts or etwas with haben, a second verb goes to the end as an infinitive with zu: Ich habe viel zu tun = I have a lot to do. Modal verbs like kann and muss are different: they take the infinitive without zu (Ich kann das tun).

examples.en: I have a lot to do.

examples.text: Das hat nichts mit dir zu tun.
examples.en: That has nothing to do with you.

concepts.title: Modal verbs in the plural: wir können
concepts.explanation: Modal verbs are irregular in the singular (ich kann, er kann, with no ending), but their plural forms are regular and match the infinitive: wir können, sie können, Sie können. The second verb still goes to the end: Was können wir tun?

concepts.title: alle vs. alles
concepts.explanation: alles means 'everything' and is singular: Alles ist gut. alle means 'everyone, all (of them)' and is plural, so the verb is plural too: Alle sind hier = Everyone is here.

concepts.title: wurde: 'became, got'
concepts.explanation: wurde is the past of werden (to become, to get). It is used for ich, er, sie and es: Es wurde mir zu viel = It got to be too much for me. Later you will also meet wurde as the helper verb for the passive ('was done').

examples.en: It got to be too much for me.

concepts.title: es gibt: 'there is / there are'
concepts.explanation: German says 'there is' and 'there are' with es gibt, literally 'it gives'. It stays gibt for one thing or many: Es gibt keine = There aren't any. The thing that exists is an object, so it goes into the accusative (einen, den).

examples.text: Es gibt noch viel zu tun.
examples.en: There's still a lot to do.

concepts.title: ihr and euch: 'you' for several people
concepts.explanation: ihr is informal 'you' for a group when it is the subject. As an object, or after words like für, mit, bei, it becomes euch: Ist das für euch? = Is that for you guys? Unlike mich/mir or dich/dir, euch is the same in the accusative and the dative.

concepts.title: machen and tun: two verbs for 'do'
concepts.explanation: Both machen and tun can mean 'to do': Was machen wir jetzt? and Was tun wir jetzt? both mean 'What do we do now?'. In everyday speech machen is more common. Only machen also means 'to make'.

examples.en: There's nothing you can do about it.

examples.text: Ich kann das für dich machen.
examples.en: I can do that for you.

concepts.title: 'Let's ...': verb first, then wir
concepts.explanation: To suggest doing something together, put the wir-form of the verb first and wir right after it, and end with an exclamation mark: Machen wir das! = Let's do it! It looks like a yes/no question, but the tone and punctuation show it is a suggestion.

concepts.title: All nouns start with a capital letter
concepts.explanation: In German every noun is written with a capital letter, not just names: Zeit (time), not zeit. This makes nouns easy to spot in a sentence: Ich habe keine Zeit.

concepts.title: Every noun has a gender: der, die, das
concepts.explanation: Each German noun is masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das), and the gender often can't be guessed from the meaning. Zeit is feminine: die Zeit, keine Zeit. Learn every noun together with its article.

concepts.title: Formal commands: verb first, then Sie
concepts.explanation: To tell someone you address as Sie to do something, use the Sie-form of the verb first, followed by Sie: Sagen Sie mir, wo er ist. = Tell me where he is. The word Sie is never left out in formal commands.

examples.text: Sagen Sie mir, wo er ist.

concepts.title: viel vs. viele: 'much' and 'many'
concepts.explanation: viel means 'much, a lot' for amounts you don't count: viel Zeit = a lot of time. viele means 'many' for things or people you can count: Wir sind viele = There are many of us. The same goes for questions: wie viel (how much) vs. wie viele (how many).

examples.en: How much time do we have?

concepts.title: nie: 'never'
concepts.explanation: nie means 'never' and goes where nicht would go: Er ist nie da (He's never around). noch nie means 'never (so far)': Ich war noch nie in Wien. nie mehr means 'never again'.

examples.text: Ich war noch nie in Wien.
Ich will nie mehr nach Paris.
examples.en: I never want to go to Paris again.

concepts.title: bitte: 'please', 'here you go', 'pardon?'
concepts.explanation: bitte means 'please' and can go at the start, at the end, or right after the verb: Kann ich bitte gehen? On its own it also means 'here you go' or 'you're welcome'. Wie bitte? means 'Pardon?' when you didn't hear something.

concepts.title: doch: 'yes' against a negative
concepts.explanation: When someone says or asks something negative and you want to disagree, answer doch instead of ja. Du hast keine Zeit? – Doch! (You don't have time? – Yes, I do!). ja would sound like you agree with the negative.

examples.text: Ich bin nicht gut. – Doch, du bist sehr gut!
examples.en: I'm not good. – Yes you are, you're very good!

concepts.title: doch as an emphasis word
concepts.explanation: Inside a sentence, doch often adds emphasis like 'you know', 'surely' or 'come on'. It has no direct translation: Das weiß ich doch! (I know that!). In commands it makes them more urgent or encouraging: Machen Sie doch etwas!

concepts.title: Feminine nouns in the dative: die becomes der
concepts.explanation: After a dative preposition like in, mit or zu, a feminine noun's article changes: die becomes der, and diese becomes dieser. So die Zeit turns into mit der Zeit (over time) or in dieser Zeit (during that time).

examples.text: In dieser Zeit war ich in Paris.
examples.en: During that time I was in Paris.

examples.text: Mit der Zeit wird alles gut.
examples.en: Over time everything will be fine.

examples.text: Zu dieser Zeit ist er nie da.
examples.en: He's never around at this time.
examples.review: 'Zu dieser Zeit ist er nie da' is slightly unidiomatic for 'at this time (of day)', where 'um diese Zeit' is normal; consider a different example such as 'Mit dieser Zeit…' or keep only the 'in' and 'mit' examples.

concepts.notes: generated by claude-opus-5-5 (tools/generate.py, 2026-11-28) | REVIEW warning: Calling 'in' a dative preposition is misleading, since it is a two-way preposition that also takes the accusative; say 'after prepositions like mit or zu (and in when it means where/when)'.

concepts.title: Relative pronouns: der, die, das = 'who, that, which'
concepts.explanation: der, die and das can also mean 'who' or 'that' and start a relative clause. A comma comes before it and the verb goes to the end: Es gibt Menschen, die das können (There are people who can do that).

examples.text: Es gibt Menschen, die das können.
examples.en: There are people who can do that.

examples.text: Das ist einer, der viel weiß.
examples.en: That's someone who knows a lot.

examples.text: Das ist eine, die alles kann.
examples.en: She's someone who can do everything.

concepts.title: The perfect tense: haben + past participle
concepts.explanation: To talk about the past in conversation, German usually uses a form of haben plus a past participle at the end of the sentence. Many participles start with ge- and end in -t: sagen becomes gesagt. Ich habe nichts gesagt means 'I didn't say anything'.

concepts.title: The passive: werden + past participle
concepts.explanation: The passive uses werden plus a past participle at the end, like English 'is / was + done'. Das wurde mir schon gesagt means 'I've already been told that'. wird is present, wurde is past.

examples.text: Mir wurde gesagt, dass er in Wien ist.
examples.en: I was told that he's in Vienna.

examples.text: Es wird gesagt, dass er viel weiß.
examples.en: It's said that he knows a lot.

concepts.title: würde + infinitive: 'would'
concepts.explanation: würde (with an umlaut) means 'would'. Like other helper verbs, it sends the infinitive to the end: Das würde ich nie tun (I would never do that). Don't mix it up with wurde, which means 'became' or 'was'.

concepts.title: Simple past of regular verbs: -te
concepts.explanation: Regular verbs form the simple past by adding -te to the stem: sagen becomes ich sagte, er sagte. The ich and er/sie/es forms are the same. It is common in writing and storytelling; in conversation Germans often use the perfect (ich habe gesagt) instead.

concepts.title: möchte: 'would like'
concepts.explanation: möchte is the polite way to say what you want: ich möchte = 'I would like'. It works like a modal verb: any second verb goes to the end as an infinitive (Ich möchte etwas sagen). The ich and er/sie/es forms are the same. With a destination, the verb of motion is often left out: Ich möchte nach Berlin.

examples.en: I'd like to go to Berlin.

concepts.title: ihr / ihre: 'her' and 'their'
concepts.explanation: The possessive ihr means both 'her' and 'their'; context tells you which. Like mein, it takes endings: ihre before feminine and plural nouns (ihre Zeit), ihr before neuter ones (ihr Leben). Capitalized Ihr / Ihre means formal 'your'.

examples.text: Wie war ihre Zeit in Rom?
examples.en: How was her time in Rome?

examples.text: Sami und Norah sagen, ihre Zeit in Rom war sehr gut.
examples.en: Sami and Norah say their time in Rome was very good.

examples.review: 'Ist das ihre?' is a standalone possessive pronoun ('hers'), but the explanation only covers the determiner use before a noun, so this example doesn't illustrate what is explained; replace it with a determiner example or add a sentence on standalone use.

concepts.notes: generated by claude-opus-5-5 (tools/generate.py, 2026-11-28) | REVIEW warning: The explanation says plain 'ihr' is used before neuter nouns only, but it is also used before masculine nouns in the nominative (ihr Vater), so learners may overgeneralise 'ihre'; suggest 'ihr before masculine and neuter nouns (ihr Leben)'.

concepts.title: Wie geht es dir? Asking how someone is
concepts.explanation: To ask how someone is, German says literally 'How goes it to you?': Wie geht es dir? The person is in the dative (mir, dir, ihm, uns), not the subject. Answer with the same pattern: Mir geht es gut = 'I'm fine'.

concepts.title: es geht um: 'it's about'
concepts.explanation: Es geht um + accusative means 'it's about' or 'what matters is'. The subject is always es: Es geht um Geld = 'It's about money'. It can also mean something is at stake: Es geht um alles.

concepts.title: hätte: 'would have', 'if I had'
concepts.explanation: hätte is the 'would' form of haben, used for things that aren't real. Ich hätte Zeit = 'I would have time'. In wenn-clauses it means 'if I had': Wenn ich Zeit hätte, ... = 'If I had time, ...'. With doch or nur it expresses a wish: Hätte ich doch mehr Zeit!

examples.text: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich mit dir gehen.
examples.en: If I had time, I'd go with you.
If only I had more time!

examples.text: Wenn ich nur mehr Geld hätte!
examples.en: If only I had more money!

concepts.title: hätte + past participle: 'would have done'
concepts.explanation: To talk about what would have happened but didn't, use hätte plus a past participle at the end, just like the perfect tense with haben. Ich habe das gesagt = 'I said that'; Ich hätte das gesagt = 'I would have said that'.

examples.en: I would never have said that.
I would have said that too.

concepts.title: Two infinitives at the end: gehen müssen
concepts.explanation: When a modal verb itself follows werden or hätte, it stands in its infinitive form at the very end, after the other verb: Ich werde gehen müssen = 'I'll have to go'. With hätte, the modal stays an infinitive instead of becoming a participle: Das hätte er sagen müssen = 'He should have said that'.

examples.en: He'll have to do a lot.

concepts.title: mal: a softener for requests
concepts.explanation: mal (short for einmal) is often added to requests and suggestions to make them sound casual and friendly, a bit like 'just' in English. It doesn't translate literally: Kannst du mal sehen? = 'Could you take a look?' Mal sehen on its own means 'Let's see.'

examples.text: Kannst du mir mal sagen, wo er ist?
examples.en: Can you just tell me where he is?

examples.text: Kannst du mal sehen, wer da ist?
examples.en: Can you go and see who's there?

concepts.title: ohne: 'without' (+ accusative)
concepts.explanation: ohne means 'without' and is always followed by the accusative, like für. So you say ohne dich, ohne mich, ohne ihn. Ohne mich! on its own means 'Count me out!'

concepts.title: ohne ... zu: 'without doing'
concepts.explanation: To say 'without doing something', German uses ohne + zu + infinitive, with the infinitive at the very end. English uses an -ing form instead: ohne etwas zu sagen = 'without saying anything'. A comma separates this part from the rest of the sentence.

examples.text: Er geht, ohne etwas zu sagen.
Sie geht, ohne mich zu sehen.
Kannst du das machen, ohne Geld zu haben?
examples.en: Can you do that without having money?

concepts.title: Commands to several people: Kommt!
concepts.explanation: To tell several friends to do something, use the ihr form of the verb and simply leave out ihr. Kommt ihr? means 'Are you coming?', while Kommt! means 'Come!' Words like bitte and doch make it softer.

concepts.title: wenn ..., dann ...: 'if ..., then ...'
concepts.explanation: After a wenn-clause you can start the main clause with dann ('then'). The verb still comes right after it: Wenn du keine Zeit hast, dann gehen wir. The dann is optional, just like 'then' in English.

examples.text: Wenn du keine Zeit hast, dann gehen wir ohne dich.
examples.en: If you don't have time, then we'll go without you.

examples.text: Wenn das so ist, dann will ich nicht.
examples.en: If that's how it is, then I don't want to.

examples.text: Wenn er nicht kommt, dann gehen wir.
examples.en: If he doesn't come, then we'll go.

concepts.title: Ihnen: formal 'you' in the dative
concepts.explanation: Formal Sie has a dative form, Ihnen, always with a capital I. Use it where du would become dir: Wie geht es dir? becomes Wie geht es Ihnen? It also follows words like mit and von: mit Ihnen.

examples.en: I have to tell you something.

concepts.title: Das macht nichts: 'it doesn't matter'
concepts.explanation: Das macht nichts (or just Macht nichts!) is the everyday way to say 'never mind, no problem'. With the separable particle aus it becomes 'to mind': Das macht mir nichts aus = 'I don't mind'.

concepts.title: zu Hause vs. nach Hause
concepts.explanation: German uses two fixed phrases for 'home'. zu Hause means 'at home' (where you are): Ich bin zu Hause. nach Hause means '(to) home' (where you're going): Ich will nach Hause. The -e in Hause is an old ending that survives only in these phrases.

concepts.title: Possessives take ein's endings: seinen
concepts.explanation: Possessive words like sein ('his') change their endings exactly like ein. When a masculine noun is the object, ein becomes einen, and sein becomes seinen: Das ist sein Tag, but Er hatte seinen Tag.

examples.text: Ich habe nur einen Tag Zeit.

concepts.title: selbst: 'myself, yourself' and 'even'
concepts.explanation: selbst never changes its form. After a verb or pronoun it adds emphasis like English '-self': Das weiß ich selbst = 'I know that myself'. At the front, before a word, it means 'even': Selbst er weiß das nicht = 'Even he doesn't know that'.

concepts.title: bis: 'until', 'up to'
concepts.explanation: bis marks an end point in time or space: bis jetzt = 'until now, so far'. With von it gives a range: von zwei bis drei = 'from two to three'. Bis dann! is a common goodbye meaning 'See you then!'

examples.en: So far everything has been fine.

examples.text: Ich habe von zwei bis drei Zeit.
examples.en: I'm free from two to three.

concepts.notes: generated by claude-opus-5-5 (tools/generate.py, 2026-11-28) | REVIEW warning: The explanation does not cover bis as a conjunction ('bis er hier ist') or its frequent combination with another preposition ('bis nach Hause'), although entry 148 uses both. Consider adding a sentence on each.

concepts.title: Frau + surname: 'Mrs.' / 'Ms.'
concepts.explanation: To address a woman politely, use Frau plus her surname, together with formal Sie: Frau Ali, haben Sie Zeit? Frau is used for all adult women, married or not, so it covers both 'Mrs.' and 'Ms.'.

examples.en: Ms. Ali, do you have time?

examples.text: Wie geht es Ihnen, Frau Ali?

concepts.title: durch takes the accusative
concepts.explanation: durch means 'through' and is always followed by the accusative, like für. You see it in pronouns and masculine nouns: durch dich, durch ihn, durch den Tag. It can also mean 'thanks to' or 'by means of': Durch dich weiß ich das.

examples.text: Durch dich weiß ich das jetzt.
examples.en: Thanks to you, I know that now.

concepts.title: Past participles ending in -en
concepts.explanation: Regular verbs form the past participle with ge- ... -t (sagen → gesagt). Many common irregular ('strong') verbs use ge- ... -en instead: sehen → gesehen. Their stem vowel sometimes changes too, so learn each participle with its verb.

concepts.title: Commands to one person (du)
concepts.explanation: When you tell one person you say du to what to do, the verb comes first and du is dropped. For most verbs you use the stem, sometimes with -e added. The verb sein is irregular: its du command is Sei! (Sei nicht so! 'Don't be like that!')

concepts.title: sei: reporting what someone said
concepts.explanation: In careful German, especially in news and writing, reported speech uses a special verb form called Konjunktiv I. For sein it is sei: Er sagte, er sei zu Hause ('He said he was at home'). It signals 'this is what they said', without claiming it's true. In everyday speech people often just use ist.

examples.text: Er sagte, er sei zu Hause.
examples.en: He said he was at home.

examples.text: Alle sagen, er sei sehr gut.

concepts.title: Leaving out dass
concepts.explanation: After verbs like sagen, wissen and glauben you can drop dass, just as English drops 'that'. Without dass the second clause keeps normal word order with the verb in second place: Ich weiß, du kannst das = Ich weiß, dass du das kannst.

examples.text: Er sagte, er sei zu Hause.
examples.en: He said he was at home.
I know you can do it.

examples.text: Sie sagte, sie hat kein Geld.
examples.en: She said she has no money.

concepts.title: wäre: 'would be', 'were'
concepts.explanation: wäre is the 'would' form of sein, like hätte for haben. It means 'would be' (Das wäre gut) and is used for unreal situations after wenn: Wenn ich du wäre ... ('If I were you ...'). You don't need würde with it.

examples.text: Wenn ich du wäre, würde ich das nicht machen.
examples.en: If I were you, I wouldn't do that.

concepts.title: glauben: dir, es, an
concepts.explanation: glauben ('believe, think') takes a person in the dative: Ich glaube dir ('I believe you'). A thing is accusative: Das glaube ich nicht. 'Believe in' is glauben an + accusative: Ich glaube an dich.

concepts.title: Modal verbs in the past: wollte
concepts.explanation: Modal verbs form their simple past with -te, like regular verbs: wollen → ich wollte, er wollte. The ich and er/sie forms are the same. As in the present, a second verb goes to the end: Er wollte nicht kommen.

concepts.title: Contractions: zur, zum, im, am
concepts.explanation: Some prepositions merge with dem or der into one word. zu + der = zur, zu + dem = zum, in + dem = im, an + dem = am. These short forms are normal and usually required: Ich muss zur Arbeit ('I have to go to work').

examples.en: I have to go to work.

concepts.title: gerade: German's '-ing' form
concepts.explanation: German has no special '-ing' tense: Was macht ihr? can mean 'What do you do?' or 'What are you doing?'. To stress that something is happening right now, add gerade: Was macht ihr gerade? With a past verb it means 'just': Ich habe ihn gerade gesehen.

examples.en: I don't have time right now.
He isn't here at the moment.
What are you doing right now?

concepts.title: denn in questions: 'then', 'so'
concepts.explanation: In questions, denn is a small flavoring word that makes the question sound more natural, curious or a bit surprised. It often has no direct English translation, or comes out as 'then' or 'so': "Wo bist du denn?" = 'So where are you?' It goes after the verb and pronouns, not at the start.

concepts.title: denn: 'because' (normal word order)
concepts.explanation: denn means 'because' and joins two main clauses. Like und and aber, it doesn't count for word order, so the verb stays in second place: "..., denn ich habe keine Zeit." denn always comes after the first clause, never at the start of the sentence.

examples.text: Ich kann nicht kommen, denn ich habe keine Zeit.
examples.en: I can't come because I don't have time.

examples.text: Er ist nicht hier, denn er ist bei der Arbeit.
examples.en: He isn't here because he's at work.

examples.text: Wir gehen nach Hause, denn wir haben kein Geld mehr.
examples.en: We're going home because we have no money left.

concepts.title: gerne: 'like to', 'gladly'
concepts.explanation: To say you like doing something, German adds gerne to the verb: "Ich bin gerne hier" = 'I like being here.' On its own, "Gerne!" means 'With pleasure!' or 'You're welcome!' With würde, hätte or möchte it makes a polite wish: "Ich hätte gerne zwei" = 'I'd like two.' The short form gern means the same.

concepts.title: dein vs. deine: matching the noun
concepts.explanation: Words for 'my, your, his' (mein, dein, sein) take the same endings as ein. Before a der or das noun (as subject) there's no ending: dein Mann, dein Haus. Before a die noun or a plural, add -e: deine Frau.

concepts.title: Comparatives: besser als
concepts.explanation: To say 'better', 'more ...', German usually adds -er to the adjective, and 'than' is als. gut is irregular, just like English good: gut, besser. "Du bist besser als ich" = 'You're better than me.'

concepts.title: Was für ein ...?: 'what kind of'
concepts.explanation: Was für ein + noun asks what kind of thing something is. The words often split up: was at the front, für ein later: "Was ist das für ein Buch?" = 'What kind of book is that?' In exclamations it means 'what a ...!': "Was für ein Tag!"

examples.text: Was ist das für ein Buch?
examples.en: What kind of book is that?

examples.text: Was für ein Mann ist er?
examples.en: What kind of man is he?

concepts.title: helfen takes the dative
concepts.explanation: Some verbs take a dative object where English just has a plain object. helfen is one of them: you help mir, dir, ihm, not mich, dich, ihn. "Kannst du mir helfen?" = 'Can you help me?'

concepts.title: soll: 'should', 'be supposed to'
concepts.explanation: soll (from sollen) is a modal verb: the infinitive goes to the end. It says what someone expects or wants you to do: "Er soll nach Hause kommen" = 'He's supposed to come home.' As a question with ich it makes an offer: "Soll ich dir helfen?" = 'Shall I help you?'

concepts.title: soll: 'is said to'
concepts.explanation: soll can also pass on something you've heard but can't confirm. "Er soll sehr viel Geld haben" = 'He's said to have a lot of money.' English uses 'supposedly', 'apparently' or 'is said to'.

examples.text: Er soll sehr viel Geld haben.
examples.en: He's said to have a lot of money.

examples.text: Das Buch soll sehr gut sein.
examples.en: The book is supposed to be very good.

examples.text: Sie soll jetzt in Paris sein.

concepts.title: mag: 'like' (+ noun)
concepts.explanation: ich mag / er mag means 'like' and usually takes a noun or pronoun: "Ich mag dich" = 'I like you.' To say you like doing something, use the verb with gerne instead: "Ich bin gerne hier." möchte ('would like') is a form of the same verb, mögen.

concepts.title: in + accusative: going into (ins)
concepts.explanation: in uses the dative for location (where?) but the accusative for movement into a place (where to?). So das Haus becomes dem Haus = im Haus when you are inside, but stays das Haus = ins Haus when you go in: Er ist im Haus (he is in the house) vs. Er geht ins Haus (he goes into the house).

examples.en: We're going into the house now.

concepts.title: keinen: kein before masculine objects
concepts.explanation: kein takes the same endings as ein. Before a masculine noun used as an object, ein becomes einen, so kein becomes keinen: Sie hat keinen Mann (she has no husband). keinen can also stand alone, meaning 'none' or 'not one'.

examples.text: Hat sie einen Mann? – Nein, sie hat keinen.
examples.en: Does she have a husband? – No, she doesn't.

concepts.title: schon lange + present: 'have been ... for a long time'
concepts.explanation: For something that started in the past and is still going on, German uses the present tense with schon, where English uses 'have been'. Ich bin schon lange hier means 'I have been here for a long time'. Don't use the perfect tense for this.

examples.en: I've been here for a long time.

examples.text: Wie lange bist du schon in Berlin?
examples.en: How long have you been in Berlin?
I've known that for a long time.

concepts.notes: generated by claude-opus-5-5 (tools/generate.py, 2026-11-28) | REVIEW warning: The flat rule 'Don't use the perfect tense for this' may confuse learners, because the same entry has 'Wir haben uns lange nicht gesehen' (perfect, correct for a negated or completed span). Suggested fix: limit the rule to states or actions still going on, e.g. 'For an ongoing state, use the present (Ich bin schon lange hier), not the perfect.'

concepts.title: Adjectives before a noun get an ending
concepts.explanation: After sein an adjective has no ending, but directly before a noun it takes an ending that matches the noun. Die Zeit ist lang, but eine lange Zeit (a long time). For now, notice the -e; the full pattern comes step by step.

examples.text: Er war lange Zeit in Paris.
examples.en: He was in Paris for a long time.

concepts.title: sprechen mit ... über ...: talk to ... about ...
concepts.explanation: You talk mit someone (dative) and über something (accusative). Kann ich mit dir sprechen? = Can I talk to you? Wir sprechen über das Buch = We're talking about the book. Don't use zu for 'talk to'.

examples.text: Wir müssen über das Geld sprechen.
examples.en: We need to talk about the money.

concepts.title: lassen + infinitive: 'let someone do'
concepts.explanation: lassen works like a modal verb: the second verb goes to the end as a plain infinitive, with no zu. Lassen Sie mich sprechen! = Let me speak! With another modal, two infinitives stack at the end: Ich kann dich nicht gehen lassen.

examples.text: Ich kann dich nicht gehen lassen.

concepts.title: meinen: 'to think' and 'to mean'
concepts.explanation: meinen means 'to mean' (Wie meinen Sie das? = What do you mean by that?) and also 'to think' in the sense of having an opinion (Was meinen Sie? = What do you think?). Careful: meinen can also be the possessive 'my' before a masculine object (meinen Mann).

examples.en: What do you mean by that?

concepts.title: Plural nouns: always die, endings vary
concepts.explanation: In the plural, the article is always die, whatever the gender: das Kind becomes die Kinder. Plural endings vary (-er, -en, -e, -s, or none), so learn each noun's plural with it: Kind → Kinder, Mensch → Menschen.

examples.en: The children are in the house.

concepts.title: Present tense for the future
concepts.explanation: German often uses the plain present tense for future plans, especially with a time word like morgen. Er kommt morgen = He's coming tomorrow / He'll come tomorrow. The werden future is possible but not needed here.

concepts.title: ob: 'whether, if' (verb at the end)
concepts.explanation: ob introduces an indirect yes/no question, like English 'whether' or 'if': Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt. Like dass, it sends the verb to the end. Use wenn for 'if' as a condition, but ob after verbs like wissen. On its own, Ob ...? means 'I wonder if ...'.

examples.text: Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt.
examples.en: I don't know if he's coming.

examples.text: Wissen Sie, ob sie zu Hause ist?
examples.en: Do you know whether she's at home?
I wonder if that's really true.
